idiom_name: pointer-to-function chain with explicit context structs
implementation_notes: C has no closures, so a step is a pointer to function - `typedef int (*step_fn)(int, void *ctx)` when it needs configuration - and composition is a hand-written helper that stores steps and applies them in order; cppreference documents pointers to functions as ordinary objects that can be stored, copied, passed and invoked. The classic composition structure therefore does not collapse: it is rebuilt per signature, a chain of chains needs another helper, and configured steps must carry their context alongside the pointer. Composing plain functions is still the right move when the same multi-step transformation is reused in several places; for one fixed chain, calling the steps in order inside a single named function is clearer and faster.
pitfalls: A function pointer carries no state: every configured step needs its own context pointer, and a shared or long-lived context makes an otherwise pure chain non-reentrant and thread-unsafe.
Storing only the pointers (a bare array of step_fn) silently drops the configuration; store the (function, context) pair.
Nothing type-checks a wrong-arity step: casting a function pointer to a mismatched signature is undefined behaviour that the compiler will not catch.
